description: Looking at a blue sky is so ordinary that we forget to ask why. The answer lies in the light of the Sun and in the air we look through to see it.

hero.hook: The sky is not painted blue: it is a magic trick performed by light and air.

blocks.text: Looking up at a blue sky is so ordinary that we forget to ask why it is blue. The **atmosphere**, the layer of gas wrapped around the Earth, has no color of its own. That shade comes from a very precise meeting between sunlight and the gas molecules floating around us.

Understanding this blue means understanding how light travels and **scatters**, that is, how it bounces off in every direction instead of running straight ahead. And here is the bonus: the same effect turns the sky red and orange at sunset.

Sunlight looks white to us, but it actually holds every color of the rainbow: that is the [[visible light spectrum]]. Each color matches a **wavelength**, the size of its light “wave.” Blue and violet have short waves; red has long ones.

On the Moon there is no air to scatter light. The result: up there the sky stays **black in broad daylight**, even with the Sun shining. Proof that the color of the sky comes from the air, not from the Sun.

Between the Sun and our eyes, the air is not empty. It is packed with tiny **gas molecules**, mostly nitrogen, about **78%** of the air, and oxygen, about **21%**. They are far smaller than the waves of light. When a ray hits them, it stops running straight and is thrown off in every direction. That little bounce is where the color of the sky begins.

In **1871**, the British physicist **Lord Rayleigh** put the effect into an equation. He found that the shorter a color's wave, the more the air molecules throw it around. This is [[Rayleigh scattering]].
The sky of Mars does the opposite of ours: its iron-rich dust makes it pink by day, while its sunsets turn **blue**. Everything depends on what the air is carrying.

blocks.caption: Blue light is scattered in every direction by the air

blocks.text: In practice, blue light is scattered about **9 times more** than red. Red crosses the air almost in a straight line, while blue ricochets everywhere. That is why, wherever you look in the sky, some blue always ends up reaching your eyes: the whole sky seems to “glow” with this scattered blue.
There is a logical objection here: if the shortest waves scatter the most, violet should win, since its wave is even shorter than blue's. And the sky does hold plenty of scattered violet.

The answer is not in the sky but in our eyes. We pick up colors with sensors called **cones**, light-sensitive cells in the retina. They are far more sensitive to blue than to violet. On top of that, the Sun sends out more blue light than violet. Our brain averages all of it and sees a clean blue. An animal tuned to other colors would probably see a completely different sky.

Sunset follows the same rules but changes one thing: distance. At midday, light crosses a thin layer of air. In the evening, with the Sun low, its rays have to cross **far more air** before they reach us.

blocks.caption: Close to the horizon, light crosses a far greater thickness of air

blocks.text: Over that long path, the blue is scattered away long before it gets to us, filtered out by the sheer depth of the air. Only the toughest colors are left, the reds and the oranges. When dust or pollution is in the way, [[Mie scattering]] takes over: particles bigger than air molecules turn the sky milky or deepen those orange tones.
The sky is blue because short waves are scattered about **9 times more** by the air than long waves. At sunset, light crosses so much air that only red still gets through to us.
